card.stem: The sketch shows the external wall and timber first floor of a dwelling house. The external wall is a 400 mm concrete block wall with a full-fill insulated cavity. The wall is plastered on both sides. The first floor joists are 225 mm × 50 mm and are fixed to the external wall using joist hangers. The floor is finished with a tongued and grooved hardwood floor, on 20 mm plywood decking with a plasterboard ceiling beneath.
card.questionText: To a scale of 1:5, draw a vertical section through the external wall and first floor. On your drawing show the typical construction details from a level 400 mm below the plasterboard ceiling to a level 400 mm above the hardwood floor. Show an internal floor width of 900 mm. Include four typical dimensions.

rows.contextNote: Credit the best SEVEN acceptable details at 5 marks each, capped at 35. Marked details: concrete block outer leaf with render; full-fill cavity with wall tie; concrete block inner leaf with internal plaster; joist hanger; joist; airtight tape; plasterboard; plywood decking; tongue and groove flooring; skirting board. The model specifies 19 mm render, 100 mm leaves, a 200 mm full-fill cavity, 15 mm plaster, 225 × 50 mm joists and 20 mm plywood decking.
Four appropriate typical dimensions on the section.

rows.verbatim: Draughting, accuracy and scale (excellent, good, fair)
rows.contextNote: Draughting, accuracy and scale of the section: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4.

card.stem: The sketch shows an old uninsulated dwelling house. The homeowner has received a grant to carry out energy upgrades to their house. They have decided to start by adding external insulation to the walls of the house.
card.questionText: Discuss two reasons why energy upgrade grants are available for old houses.

rows.contextNote: Such as: to improve the BER of the house; to reduce the energy use of the home and so its carbon emissions.

A second, different reason. Such as: to encourage owners to upgrade existing houses instead of building new ones; to make older houses energy efficient, sustainable and economical to heat; to encourage greener living.

card.stem: The sketch shows an old uninsulated dwelling house. The homeowner has received a grant to carry out energy upgrades to their house. They have decided to start by adding external insulation to the walls of the house.
card.questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, show one suitable method of applying an external insulation system to a house. Specify the type and thickness of insulation.

rows.verbatim: Method of insulating external walls note & sketch (8 + 8 marks)
rows.contextNote: Note 8 and sketch 8 of one method. Such as: clean the wall; fix starter tracks at DPC level; apply adhesive to the back and perimeter of the boards and stagger their joints; fix with mechanical anchors; apply a 6–10 mm polymer-modified base render with glass-fibre mesh lapped at least 100 mm; then a final finish.

rows.verbatim: Preferred insulation type for external wall
rows.contextNote: Such as: expanded polystyrene (EPS), phenolic, polyisocyanurate (PIR) or extruded polystyrene (XPS).
The scheme recommends a 200 mm insulation thickness.

card.questionText: State two specific safety precautions to be observed in the Construction Studies classroom in each of the following situations: using a jigsaw; using epoxy adhesive.

rows.contextNote: Such as: wear a dust mask; wear ear protection; wear eye protection against dust and flying chips.
A second, different jigsaw precaution. Such as: keep leads from being a trip hazard; secure the work piece against movement.
Such as: work in a well-ventilated zone; protect skin and clothing.
A second, different epoxy precaution. Such as: a respirator mask against the vapours; eye protection; keep the work area clear to avoid slips if the epoxy leaks.

card.questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: concrete mixer; smart radiator valve; ridge tile; triple glazing; balusters; cedar cladding; bridle joint; wood pellet stove; floor screed.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Concrete mixer: a rotating drum that turns raw materials into concrete without segregation; small on-site batch mixers (electric, petrol or diesel) are hand loaded and make up to 200 litres per batch, so quality control is difficult; larger quantities come from a mixing plant in a ready-mix truck of 4–6 cubic metres, better regulated and poured directly into the work area. Smart radiator valve: fitted to new or existing radiators; integrated sensors measure the room temperature and signal to reduce or increase the flow of hot water; controlled from smart devices when the owners are away; each room can have its own temperature; reduces energy cost and use. Ridge tile: sits on the apex of the roof and seals the intersection of the two roof planes; traditionally bedded in mortar, now often fixed with integrated dry-fix systems; made from materials like the roof covering, in a variety of colours and profiles. Triple glazing: three panes of glass with cavities usually filled with an inert gas (argon, xenon or krypton); reduces noise and insulates better than double glazing; heavier and thicker, so it may not suit all frames; it can reduce solar gain, so some owners avoid it on the southern elevation. Balusters: vertical members between the handrail and string of a stairs, also called spindles; moulded, square or lathe-turned; must not let a 100 mm diameter sphere pass between them; made of wood, iron or plastic. Cedar cladding: naturally durable, lasting over 60 years without preservative treatment, which is only needed to avoid the weathered silver-grey colour; fixed horizontally or vertically to battens with stainless steel or galvanised fixings, as cedar reacts with ferrous metals; low embodied energy. Bridle joint: a common, strong woodworking joint with a large gluing area; a tee or corner bridle, removing one third of the material from one piece and two thirds from the other; used in frame construction and to join table rails to uprights. Wood pellet stove: heats a home by burning renewable pellets of compressed sawdust and waste wood; an auger feeds fuel steadily from a hopper for a constant flame needing little adjustment; a low-cost heating alternative with very low emissions and a smaller environmental impact. Floor screed: the final layer of the floor on which a floor finish is laid; traditionally sand and cement at 3:1 to 5:1, levelled with a tamping board; modern free-flowing calcium sulphate screeds self-level and suit underfloor heating, at 50–75 mm over pipes clipped to the rigid insulation.
